triage.author: Benjamin Scott
triage.text: Drove hours out of my way to the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora—because let’s be real, there’s not much else pulling people through that stretch of North Dakota. Got turned away at the door for not having a timed ticket. Explained the long drive, asked if there was any way to work with us, and the staff member looked almost insulted that I’d even asked. I’ve visited presidential libraries and the Smithsonian on the Fourth of July without this nonsense. You’re not the Louvre out there, folks. A little North Dakota hospitality would’ve gone a long way.

triage.author: Den Mac
triage.text:
I have to keep reminding myself this place only opened in July. The concept is good and the place is beautiful. However, there are flow issues inside. There needs to be better signage to match the map for timeline accuracy visiting of the different areas.
While there are a lot of beautiful artifacts, the description placards contain too small of print & some of the placards have words worn off already.
In the gift shop, I think maybe they didn't plan to be so busy because they were sold out of some basic items such as TR Library stickers.

In the cafe, they could be more efficient if they would have a menu visible from the line instead of not until you get to the counter. Very beautiful grounds and conveniently located near the Medora Musical.

triage.author: cdb
triage.text:
We visited on a Sunday at the end of October.  The Library is a beautiful facility in a serene setting.  The exterior blends in splendidly with the natural landscape.

We arrived early and sat inside in comfy chairs by huge picture windows.  I bought postcards first thing while there was no one in the gift shop.  Items are spendy, the postcards were $2.99 each.  There was no price by the display and thanks to the clerk, she made sure I knew how much I was going to be charged.  When it was our appointed time to enter the exhibits, there was a throng of people getting their pictures taken at the AI photo stations. We bypassed that option and started our visit.

My overall impression was favorable, although there were several letdowns for me.
CROWD SIZE:  Having just opened in July, this attraction is drawing sizable crowds and every display had people standing side by side to view display items and it was not easy to walk between the exhibit cases.  I could tell a lot of thought went into all the exhibits, but I was only able to see a few items without reading the information.  My advice is to check the website and see when there are a lot of unreserved times - I think that would allow for more 'elbow room' and the ability to take in the displays.
We experienced several of the themed rooms and they were all in working order and still had a new feeling.  I enjoyed the room where Teddy answered questions.
THE RESTROOM:  This was a serious disappointment and worth revision consideration by the organization.  I cannot speak to the restroom configuration by the cafe, but the one in the exhibit area had to have been someone's minimalist brainchild.  The stalls were arranged in a small area and were unisex. I think there were four regular stalls and one ADA.  When I got into a stall, either the man before me or another user had peed on the seat.  My husband said the one he used was in the same shape.  The common sink area could accommodate two people comfortably while stall users moved out into the sink space.  I get the concept, but separate restrooms are the way to go.  I cannot remember if there would have been room to plumb a urinal in each of the stalls.
FINDING THE EXIT:  OMG, when we'd pegged out our fun meter and wanted to leave, we had a dickens of a time finding the exit.  I can honestly say when we finally saw the signage, it was small and up high.  I would be interested to know what the emergency exit strategy is when it might be necessary to move several hundred people out of a crowded area.  The map we received at the start of our visit was of no help.  We looked for a docent to get help, but could not locate one.
GOOD TO KNOW:  I use walking poles for balance and had no problem with the ability to use them in this facility.  There was a water fountain with a water bottle filling station, so I assumed I could have brought my own water bottle.  People were wearing sling pouches/purses, so that would have been an option since the website specifically forbids backpacks.  Non-flash photography is fine.
DEFINITELY WORTH A SECOND VISIT:  I imagine as time goes by, visitation will relax and it will be easier to see what's on display inside the Library.  We'll give it a try again during the off season.  Personally we would avoid visiting in spring and summer.  We'll visit again in fall.

triage.author: Kori N.
triage.text:
just now
Such an amazing experience! The Library left us speechless...the setting, the facilities and the separate viewing/learning areas were incredibly well done. The interactive exhibits were enjoyed by visitors of all ages, bringing history to life while featuring their own faces. Very cool, even for those of us who are not especially photogenic. Even history buffs will learn more about this extraordinary President.

There were only a couple of things could be improved. The "cafe" was close to being self-serve and the staffers were very impersonal, as in "would rather be anywhere else but there". The menu offerings were minimal and overpriced for what we received. The seating area was tight and there was a gentleman in a wheelchair who had to have assistance to free himself from the tables.

Parking was plentiful, many with coverings, but is located a fair distance from the entrance. The designers provided a small driveway for visitors needing a closer drop-off. Unfortunately, it was blocked by a Coca-Cola delivery truck (with the driver in the truck who refused to move) so we, and the vehicles behind us, had to back out of the drive and return to the open parking lot.  Pretty unacceptable and a black mark on an otherwise extraordinary experience.

We appreciated the architecture, the thoughtful layout and plentiful places to just sit and enjoy. The Theodore Roosevelt Presidental Library is a "must see" and we could not recommend this more!

triage.author: Salad Days Sally
triage.title: A Patriotic, Totally Worthwhile Experience!
triage.text: A Patriotic, Totally Worthwhile Experience! Having never before been to a presidential library, I wasn't sure what to expect. Being that it took 100 years for the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library to come to fruition after Teddy's term of office, I expected a pretty great experience. That's a long run-up. Indeed, every aspect of the library is impressive and it exceeded my expectations. The library opened in June 2026, I believe. We went in September 2026. Advanced reservations were a must. Check the website and see if they are still totally sold out. At some point, I reckon things will slow down. Not only was the library filled to capacity, but school groups also enjoyed their morning there, which I was very glad to see. Bring the young people here to learn about democracy, I say. Anyhow, let's start with the exterior and getting there. The library is located within Theodore Roosevelt National Park in Medora, North Dakota, so first you drive through the national park, enjoy the bison, prairie dogs, etc, then you follow the signs to the library along the newly paved winding road. Allow a good half hour for all this. Then, at the library, parking lots abound, so if you cannot find parking right away, chances are you will find a spot in another lot. I noted several bicycle racks in the parking lot, too, so hats off to those people who have the quadriceps and lung power to carry themselves up to the library that way. And, even better: there's a Little Free Library in the parking lot on the walk to the main building. Do you know what these are? A Little Free Library looks like a bird house at eye-level, perched on a 4x4, with the capacity to hold maybe 20 books. You can take one for free, and you can also leave one, which is a nice thing to do. If I had known about this, I would have brought a book to add. The exterior of the library has several long, unshaded, boardwalks and paths, flat and wheelchair accessible, with nice views. Some viewing areas are not yet complete and they are blocked off with caution tape. Some viewing areas have benches, again unshaded. The plantings on the walk up to the library are lovely, as are the living roof and some shaded swings on the sidewalk. At the back of the complex, you can sit on the rocking chairs and look out at the badlands and imagine Teddy enjoying the views, too. Inside the museum, you go through a metal detector and bag check. Then you snake around the lobby, past the ticket desks in the long queue. The woman at the ticket desk, having nothing to do, since everyone had an advance ticket, was there as a tour guide, giving us background on the architecture of the "rammed earth" construction of the interior. This was great - a two minute rundown of the notable features of the interior. We edged our way to the actual ticket taker, a rotund young man with round glasses. I had to wonder if he had the round glasses before he took the job, or if he chose the glasses after he landed the job. Nevertheless, he looked quite on point. He gave us each a wrist band with a computer chip. As you walk through each exhibit in each room, you can hold up your wrist with the computer chip where indicated, and it will create and track a personal diary for you as you travel throughout the museum. The diary is then sent to your email at the end of the experience as a memento. Very clever. I know I haven't even discussed the inside of the library yet... Once you receive your bracelet/ wrist band, you walk past bathrooms. Hallelujah. And lockers. And there are screens flanking the walls where you must check in with your personal information, such as your name and email, and a photo of your face. This becomes the way that the exhibits "understand" how to interact with you. The tech is amazing. The rooms begin with President Roosevelt's childhood, interests in the natural world, his presidency, his interests and advocacy, important quotes, photos, mementos (including a particularly moving display case with the shirt with bullet hole and other items from the day he was shot - I won't spoil the details on that if you don't know how his life was saved. It's worth checking out - see my photo), his exploration of the Amazon River after his presidency, his legacy, and room with a moving video with many well-known people's voices narrating, another room with your own name and some significant details that appear in a constellation of a night sky (again, thanks to the wonders of technology, this is quite impressive, and I won't spoil the significance of this activity). There's a playroom where young kids can climb around. It seems they really thought of everything. But what I enjoyed the most was the exhibit room that is set up like President Roosevelt's office in the White House, replete with a three dimensional AI Theodore Roosevelt who will interact with you! When you walk into his office, you stand behind the desk, start the motion happening by tapping your bracelet on the right spot, and then you can ask a question into the microphone, which Teddy will answer, sometimes using your name. So, readers, educate yourselves! Read a book on Teddy Roosevelt before going here so that you will have questions to ask. I read "Death on the River of Doubt" and had several questions to ask, which he answered fairly well or very well. This was so much fun. Other people walked in and out of this exhibit space, not having any questions prepared. Don't be shy, I thought. But, since nobody else had questions to ask, I monopolized him for a good five minutes, I'd reckon. Anyhow, this was a highlight. We opted to skip the film, but that is an option. The gift shop area, back at the library entrance, has a nice selection of items, and the restaurant around the back, behind the bathroom and locker area, has plenty of tables and a surprisingly good menu. The email message with the "diary" of all that we experienced that day at the library is quite impressive. I am so glad we went here, and I could have spent far more than the three hours we afforded ourselves.

7.headline: Ratings holding at 4.87 across 45 reviews
paragraphs: 45 reviews in the last 7 days, up 16 on the previous 7 days. The average is up 0.32. 2.2% rated three stars or below.

Visitors are consistently praising the interactive exhibits, the building and the setting. The AI experience continues to divide a small minority: 94 reviews to date name it as the reason for a low rating, against heavy praise for the same feature. Low volume, but it is the most likely subject of a critical feature story.

The complaints that cost us stars cluster tightly. The most frequent is the reaction against the AI experience (1 mention). These are operational and messaging fixes rather than problems with the experience itself, which is the better problem to have. Separately, 11 reviews are waiting on a reply and 5 are past our own service level.
